1. 
ADAPSO's Reasoning. The key portion of ADAPSO (which is 
technically dictum) equates the standard of review for factual questions under 
the “substantial evidence” and “arbitrary and capricious” standards. The 
question is important because Section 706(2)(E) contains an express standard 
of review for factual findings in proceedings under sections 556 and 557, i.e., 
formal proceedings. Section 706 does not contain an express standard of review 
for factual findings in informal proceedings, which means that the “catchall” 
“arbitrary and capricious” standard appfies. The structure of Section 706 
naturally raises the question whether the standard of review for factual 
findings is different for informal and formal proceedings.
ADAPSO said the standard is no different. Had then-Judge Scalia decided 
otherwise, the same facts found in the agency’s formal adjudication and in the 
agency’s notice-and-comment rulemaking would have been subject to different 
standards of review. The court rejected that approach. But in turn, the court’s 
approach threatens to render the “substantial evidence” provision of the APA 
redundant. Why would Congress have included the “substantial evidence” 
provision in Section 706 if the “arbitrary and capricious” provision already did 
all the necessary work? The court’s answer was that Congress included the 
“substantial evidence” provision in Section 706 “to emphasize that in the case 
of formal proceedings the factual support must be found in the closed record as 
opposed to elsewhere.”
2. 
ADAPSO in Other Courts. No Supreme Court case squarely resolves 
the precise question raised in ADAPSO. That question is thus governed by 
precedents from the courts of appeals.
ADAPSOs reasoning is settled law in the D.C. Circuit. See, e.g., Phoenix 
Herpetological Society, Inc. v. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, 998 F.3d 999,1005- 
06 (D.C. Cir. 2021). An example of a case applying ADAPSO is Safe Extensions, 
Inc. V. Federal Aviation Administration, 509 F.3d 593 (D.C. Cir. 2007). Under 
federal law, the FAA can “prescribe minimum safety standards for ... 
operating an airport serving any passenger . .. aircraft designed for at least 31 
passenger seats,” and “promote safe flight of civil aircraft ... by prescribing 
. . . regulations and minimum standards for . . . practices, methods, and 
procedure[s] the [agency] finds necessary for safety in air commerce.” Using 
this provision, the FAA issued an “advisory circular” making stricter the 
required test for fights that fine airport runways and the metal bases in which 
those fights sit. In Safe Extensions, a company argued that the FAA had 
arbitrarily and capriciously imposed the stricter test on its products, but not 
on other similar products of its competitors. Writing for the court. Judge Tatel
